opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what I valued most was the intellectual honesty. When you're in a room with DeepMind researchers, nobody cares about your title or how long you've been at the company. They care whether the idea is right. You could be a data center engineer like me, coming from a mechanical background, and if you had a good insight about how the cooling plant actually behaves, they'd take it seriously. And if your idea was wrong, they'd tell you, very politely but very clearly. I found that incredibly refreshing.

The second thing was the ambition. These are people who are used to working on problems where nobody knows whether a solution exists. That changes how you think. In industrial engineering we're trained to be conservative, to rely on rules of thumb and safety margins, which is the right instinct when you're running critical infrastructure. But the DeepMind folks would ask, "Why do we assume this is the best we can do?" Pairing that mindset with our operational knowledge is what made the work interesting.

And third, the rigor around evaluation. They were obsessive about measuring whether something actually worked, not just whether it looked good in a demo. When you're putting AI in control of a real physical system, where mistakes cost money or worse, that discipline matters. So the collaboration really was complementary. We brought domain expertise and a respect for safety and reliability, and they brought world-class learning algorithms and a fearlessness about tackling hard problems. Neither side could have done it alone, and that lesson has stuck with me ever since.

r001.rationale: The response describes intellectual honesty, ambition, and rigorous evaluation, but does not characterize the collaboration as a preview of technology years into the future.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what I value most is that they let me be the person who doesn't understand everything in the room. When I was at Google and we started the data center cooling project with DeepMind, I was coming from the operations side. I'd spent years thinking about chillers and cooling towers and PUE, and the researchers I was working with were thinking about reinforcement learning and model uncertainty. Neither of us could do the other's job, and nobody pretended otherwise.

That turned out to be the whole thing. The best collaborations I've seen there happen when the researcher is genuinely curious about the messy physical reality, when they want to know why a pump fails or why an operator overrides the setpoint at 3am, and the domain person is willing to say "I don't know if this will work, let's find out." At DeepMind there's a real culture of taking the problem seriously rather than taking the method seriously. They're not attached to a particular technique. If the simplest model works, great.

The other piece is rigor. A lot of applied work in industry gets rushed, and you end up deploying something you can't explain. The researchers I worked with were almost stubborn about understanding what the system was actually doing before trusting it with real equipment. When you're controlling something that can break physical infrastructure, you want that stubbornness. It was slower in the short term, and it was absolutely the right instinct.

And frankly, it's just fun. You get to sit across from people who are smarter than you about something, and they treat your expertise as equally real. That combination is rarer than it should be.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes collaboration, rigor, and mutual respect, but does not say that working with DeepMind researchers gives a technologist a preview of technology years into the future.

astra-6.text: What I really value is the curiosity and the willingness to question assumptions. You can bring a practical problem to a researcher, and they’ll ask a question that makes you realize you’ve been framing it too narrowly. I enjoy that exchange—bringing real-world constraints into the research, while letting the research change how we think about the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity, questioning assumptions, and an exchange between practical problems and research. It does not characterize the work as a preview of technology years into the future.

I really enjoy that exchange between research and engineering—taking an ambitious idea and figuring out how to make it useful in the real world.
